newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil to set up panel to help trace Nazi gold.
newsitem.headline: Brazil to set up panel to help trace Nazi gold.

text.p: The Brazilian government has agreed to set up a commission to probe the suspected transfer into the country of gold and cash belonging to Holocaust victims by fugitive Nazis after the Second World War, a government spokesman said on Tuesday.

Presidential spokesman Sergio Amaral said the government of President Fernando Henrique Cardoso would do everything in its power to trace the funds of up to 1,200 Nazis whom the government suspects fled to Brazil from Europe after 1945.
Amaral said investigators would have access to files of the state Banco do Brasil, which served as Brazil's central bank at the time the Nazi funds entered the country.

Brazilian Jewish leaders said they were pleased by the government's commitment to investigate the amount, the nature and the whereabouts of the Nazi money, much of which they suspect was plundered from millions of Jewish victims of the concentration camps.
"I know that they mean business," Henry Sobel, Senior Rabbi of Sao Paulo's Jewish Congregation said of the Cardoso's administration's promise to investigate the trail of Nazi gold.
Sobel said he had first approached Cardoso with the idea of creating a commission to probe Nazi funds in Brazil after returning from the Oslo World Jewish Council meeting in November.
"The president was very sensitive and told us Brazil had nothing to hide," Sobel said in a telephone interview.
"He said it served Brazil's purpose to distance itself from the moral stain that was the Holocaust," Sobel said.
Thousands of fugitive Nazis are suspected of having fled to Brazil, Paraguay and Argentina in the closing years of the war and under the protection of pro-Axis governments in place there at the time.

Although Brazil declared war on Germany in 1943 and even sent troops which fought in the Italian Campaign, Getulio Vargas, the Brazilian president at the time, was a fascist sympathiser and historians say he only joined the Allies under pressure from the United States.
Sobel said the Brazilian government's policy after the war was not to protect the Nazi refugees. "But they did not go out of their way to identify and arrest them either," he said.
One of the better known Nazis who lived comfortably in Brazil until he died in 1979 was Josef Mengele, a doctor at the Auschwitz concentration camp who performed experiments on inmates.

Sobel said the members of the government commission would be announced on Feb. 27, but that besides noted accountants and at least two government representatives the group would also include two senior members of the Brazilian-Jewish community.
"We the Jews of Brazil are very much interested in this process which will hopefully make all Brazilians aware of the atrocities which took place 60 years ago," he said.
